news_summary: The US science academy is advocating for faster correction of errors in scientific journals to enhance research accuracy and integrity.
news_summary_fr: L'Académie des sciences des États-Unis préconise une correction plus rapide des erreurs dans les revues scientifiques afin d'améliorer la précision et l'intégrité de la recherche.
news_summary_es: La Academia de Ciencias de EE. UU. aboga por una corrección más rápida de los errores en las revistas científicas para mejorar la precisión y la integridad de la investigación.

articles.title: US science academy urges journals to fix errors more quickly
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03787-5Long-awaited report makes recommendations for strengthening the reliability of the scientific record.
articles.content:
A statue of Albert Einstein holding a scientific manuscript sits outside the US National Academy of Sciences building in Washington DC.Credit: Paul J. Richards/AFP via Getty

Science publishers take too long to retract or correct research papers, a report by the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) finds. Standards for fixing errors are also inconsistently applied across research journals, it says.

Why retractions data could be a powerful tool for cleaning up science

There are no data on how long retraction or correction currently takes, as journals do not generally disclose when they were alerted to a problem in a paper; the NASEM report says they should. On average, according to the Retraction Watch database, retractions occur around 2.4 years after a paper is published. The report recommends that editorial review processes be completed within 12 weeks for most cases and should rarely stretch beyond 6 months — at least when editors are looking at concerns over a single paper.

“The big picture is, the process is too slow,” says Randy Schekman, a cell biologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who chaired the 14-person committee that produced the NASEM report. A prompter and more transparent process would strengthen the reliability of the scientific record, he says.

The report was due to be published online on 19 November, but publication was delayed after journalists at Science noted that it contained some references with fabricated first names for authors, a possible sign that large language models had been used to write or edit the material and had been insufficiently checked.

“It's unfortunate that there were these flawed references in a report about fixing the literature,” says Jennifer Byrne, a cancer researcher and research integrity sleuth at the University of Sydney who first flagged the concern to Science when reviewing the report, which was shared ahead of publication with media outlets.

Fixing the literature

The report had two main aims: to speed up the process of retraction or correction and to lower the “tremendous emotional barriers” for authors to correct honest mistakes in the record, Schekman says. “Part of the problem is that it’s too rare for a paper to be retracted,” he adds.

Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

The report also suggests that journals shouldn’t just wait for complaints to reach them, but instead “take proactive steps” to identify errors and integrity issues. That might include journal-wide audits, or regularly monitoring social media and online platforms where post-publication issues are raised, it says.

Existing guidelines for publishers, such as those from the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) in London, only urge a “timely” response to concerns without setting out expected schedules, and don’t suggest journals scan online platforms for complaints.

“A major theme running through the report is that we have to distinguish between retraction or correction, and research misconduct,” notes Dorothy Bishop, a research-integrity sleuth in Oxford, UK, who was on the NASEM committee. Authors shouldn’t associate retracting a paper with the stigma of misconduct, she says. And although journal editors sometimes wait for a university to investigate whether there is research misconduct before correcting a paper, they shouldn’t, she adds.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

Calls for changing these attitudes aren’t new: journals have long emphasized that retractions can cover honest mistakes. When it comes to journal processes, Holden Thorpe, the editor in chief of Science, urged that issuing corrections or retractions and making a determination of misconduct be separated in an editorial in 2022, and COPE guidelines already emphasize the point. But “there are still plenty of people who see a correction or retraction as an allegation of fraud,” says Thorpe, who was also on the NASEM committee. “Hopefully, this report will accelerate the recognition of the distinction,” he says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant and actionable recommendation by a major scientific body to improve the reliability and integrity of scientific research by speeding up corrections and retractions. This has broad positive implications for the scientific community and society by enhancing trust in scientific literature and reducing the spread of erroneous information. The report provides detailed context and concrete suggestions, addressing a systemic issue with wide-reaching impact.
articles.personality_title: US science academy calls for faster corrections to research papers
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientific research papers sometimes contain errors, but fixing these mistakes can take a long time. The US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) studied how quickly journals correct or remove flawed research.

**What happened** – In November 2026, NASEM released a report showing that journals often take years to correct or retract papers after problems are found. The report recommends that these fixes should happen within 12 weeks and rarely take more than 6 months. It also suggests journals should actively look for errors instead of waiting for complaints.

**Impact** – This is important because slow corrections can allow wrong information to spread and be used by others. The report points out that fixing honest mistakes should not be seen as shameful or linked to misconduct. Faster and clearer corrections will help make scientific research more trustworthy.

**What's next step** – Journals and publishers may adopt these recommendations to speed up their correction processes. They might also start monitoring online discussions to find problems sooner. This could lead to more reliable science that is corrected quickly when mistakes happen.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The US science academy urges journals to fix errors in research papers faster to improve trust in scientific knowledge.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’académie américaine des sciences demande d’accélérer la correction des articles scientifiques
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les articles scientifiques peuvent contenir des erreurs, mais leur correction prend souvent beaucoup de temps. L’Académie nationale des sciences, de l’ingénierie et de la médecine des États-Unis (NASEM) a étudié la rapidité avec laquelle les revues corrigent ou retirent les recherches erronées.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En novembre 2026, la NASEM a publié un rapport montrant que les revues mettent souvent plusieurs années à corriger ou retirer un article après la découverte d’un problème. Le rapport recommande que ces corrections soient faites en 12 semaines, et rarement plus de 6 mois. Il suggère aussi que les revues cherchent activement les erreurs au lieu d’attendre des plaintes.

**Impact** – C’est important car des corrections lentes peuvent laisser circuler des informations fausses. Le rapport souligne que corriger une erreur honnête ne doit pas être stigmatisé ni associé à une faute grave. Des corrections plus rapides et plus claires renforceront la confiance dans la recherche scientifique.

**Prochaine étape** – Les revues pourraient adopter ces recommandations pour accélérer leurs processus de correction. Elles pourraient aussi surveiller les discussions en ligne pour détecter les problèmes plus tôt. Cela pourrait rendre la science plus fiable et corrigée rapidement en cas d’erreur.

**Une phrase clé** – L’académie américaine des sciences demande aux revues de corriger plus vite les erreurs dans les articles pour renforcer la confiance dans le savoir scientifique.
articles.personality_title_es: La academia científica de EE.UU. pide acelerar la corrección de artículos de investigación
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los artículos científicos a veces contienen errores, pero corregirlos suele tardar mucho tiempo. La Academia Nacional de Ciencias, Ingeniería y Medicina de EE.UU. (NASEM) analizó qué tan rápido las revistas corrigen o retiran investigaciones con fallas.

**Qué pasó** – En noviembre de 2026, NASEM publicó un informe que muestra que las revistas suelen tardar años en corregir o retirar artículos tras detectar problemas. El informe recomienda que estas correcciones se hagan en 12 semanas y rara vez tarden más de 6 meses. También sugiere que las revistas busquen activamente errores en vez de esperar quejas.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque las correcciones lentas permiten que se difunda información equivocada. El informe señala que corregir errores honestos no debe verse como algo vergonzoso ni asociado a mala conducta. Correcciones más rápidas y claras ayudarán a que la ciencia sea más confiable.

**Próximo paso** – Las revistas podrían adoptar estas recomendaciones para acelerar sus procesos de corrección. También podrían vigilar discusiones en línea para detectar problemas antes. Esto podría hacer que la ciencia sea más confiable y se corrija rápido cuando haya errores.

**Una frase clave** – La academia científica de EE.UU. pide a las revistas que corrijan más rápido los errores en los artículos para aumentar la confianza en el conocimiento científico.
